Starting care

Your First Therapy Session: What to Ask and Bring

Prepare for a first therapy appointment without rehearsing your life story. Separate an introduction from clinical care and ask about goals, privacy and next steps.

About 2 minutes of article reading. Educational information, not a personal assessment.

Review draft. This article has not received clinical and publication approval.

On this page

  1. You are starting a conversation, not giving a performance
  2. Prepare a short starting note, not your complete history
  3. Leave with clarity about the next step
  4. At M.F.T.: an introduction is not a clinical session

Take these questions with you

  • What would be useful for you to know first?
  • How will you explain confidentiality and its limits?
  • What are the next step and expected costs?

No answers are collected on this page.

You are starting a conversation, not giving a performance

NIMH recommends asking about a therapist's experience, approach, fees and how treatment will proceed. Its visit-preparation guidance suggests bringing questions and information about symptoms, recent changes and medications. Those are ways to start a useful conversation; you do not need to arrive with your own diagnosis.

You may want to explain what prompted you to reach out now, what daily life has been like, and what you hope would be different. Ask the clinician what information they need at this stage and how they handle topics you are not ready to describe in detail.

Background sources [1] [2]

Prepare a short starting note, not your complete history

Here is an optional way to organize your thoughts privately: name one reason you booked, one example from everyday life, and one question about the process. A starting note might say that work stress is following you home, that you are having difficulty shifting out of it, and that you want to know how therapy could be structured. This is an illustration, not a diagnostic checklist.

Add practical needs that would help you participate, such as questions about accessibility, language, session pace or telehealth. Keep sensitive details for the clinician's approved intake process rather than placing them in advertising links, public website forms or ordinary scheduling notes.

Leave with clarity about the next step

You can ask what the clinician understands so far, what still needs to be assessed, and what they suggest happens next. Ask how you will revisit your goals and how to raise a concern about the fit. You are allowed to need clarification rather than immediately deciding that this is the right clinician.

Check the practical arrangements as well: the appointment you are requesting, expected costs, cancellation rules, privacy limits, and the appropriate route for between-session questions. Request an explanation of anything unclear in the consent materials. This page does not replace those materials or establish the terms of care.

At M.F.T.: an introduction is not a clinical session

Our free individual meet-and-greet is a brief phone introduction. A clinical first appointment has a different purpose. Ask which starting option you are requesting, and confirm the service and cost before booking. A scheduling request alone is not a confirmed appointment.
